Book Four: The Animal Soul and Its Powers
passage-en-00573

Fourth, they compare this with imagined images. We can imagine a sea of mercury or a mountain of ruby. These images are distinct and affect the soul, so they must exist somewhere, even though they do not exist outside us. The same goes for the huge and frightening images people with certain illnesses see. If such images exist in a bodily part, then a huge thing can be imprinted in a small place, so sight could work the same way. If the soul perceives them, that raises a problem: first, they themselves have argued that the soul cannot perceive particular things. Second, if images of imagined and visible things can be present in a soul that has no size or volume, then it should be even easier for a huge image to be imprinted in a small body. Third, if images can be imprinted in the soul, then imprinting is possible, and the only remaining dispute would be about where the image is imprinted.
Book Four: The Animal Soul and Its Powers
passage-en-00574

The first objection is very weak. A small body and a large one may allow endless division, but that does not make them equal in size or in the size of their parts. The second is answered by the fact that sight happens at once; it does not compare and infer. The third fails because images are not imprinted in a mirror either. Something else causes us to see what appears there, as will be explained. As for the fourth, we do not think imagined images or the images seen in illness exist in a bodily place or inside the soul. They are free-floating forms that the soul brings forth and sustains as long as they are seen. What the argument proves is only that the soul cannot be the place where particular images are stored, and that the thinking power does not perceive particular things by itself in its immaterial state. It does not prove that every act of perception happens because an image settles inside the perceiver.
Book Four: The Animal Soul and Its Powers
passage-en-00575

There is no proof that every act of perception happens by an image settling in the very being of the person who perceives it. Nor does the comparison help: it is no more reasonable for a huge image to be imprinted in something small than in something without size, especially since we have established that the soul is not the place where imagined images are stored.
Book Four: The Animal Soul and Its Powers
passage-en-00576

It is clear that two measurable things are either equal in size or one is larger than the other. If one is larger, the extra part lies outside the smaller one, so a large measure cannot be imprinted in a smaller measure. But the case of something without measure is different. Many have missed this distinction. That is why the author of The Discussions objected to the Shaykh and his followers: since they allow matter, which has no size of its own, to be the subject of all sizes, how can they argue against sight by imprinting on the ground that imagined images are present in the imagination or soul? If an image can be imprinted in the soul, they say, why not in the eye? Imprinting a large image in a small place seems easier than imprinting one in something without size.
Book Four: The Animal Soul and Its Powers
passage-en-00577

I say there is a difference between something that is definitely without size, such as a point or the soul itself, and a line or surface in some respects; and something that is not yet determined as having size or having none, but can take on either from outside. Matter considered apart from any particular form is like this: it can receive any size, and in itself it is equally open to having or not having size, because it has no fixed nature of its own. This is different from something already defined as having no size, like a point, or a particular kind of size, like a line or a tiny mustard seed. A point cannot receive any size; a line cannot receive the size of a surface or body; a mustard seed cannot receive a huge size. But matter not yet given a particular form can receive any size.
Book Four: The Animal Soul and Its Powers
passage-en-00578

The second argument is that, if sight happened by imprinting, we could not tell near from far. If what we saw were an image imprinted in the eye, that image would be the same whether the object were near or far. Just as we cannot tell by sight alone whether one of two bodies before us is near and the other far, they say, so we should not be able to sense distance. But we do sense it, so sight cannot happen by imprinting. The reply is: why could images of long and short distances not also be imprinted in us? That would allow us to perceive distance.
Book Four: The Animal Soul and Its Powers
passage-en-00579

The third argument is this: if the crystalline fluid is colorless, it should not take on shapes or colors, just as air does not. If it has a color, two impossible things follow. First, its color would mix with the color of the visible object, so we would not sense the object's color. Second, the shape and color imprinted on its surface would not pass through to the meeting point of the optic nerves behind it. A colored body with a shape imprinted on it does not pass that image through to what is behind it.
Book Four: The Animal Soul and Its Powers
passage-en-00580

The fourth argument is that if visible images were imprinted in the crystalline fluid, we should be able to sense the image in it, just as we can see green light reflected from an object onto a wall. But when we look at the image in another person's crystalline fluid, its position seems to change as we move. If it were imprinted there, its place would be fixed. Since its apparent place changes with the viewer's position, they conclude that the image is not imprinted in the fluid.
Book Four: The Animal Soul and Its Powers
passage-en-00581

I say these two arguments are strong against those who claim that the image of the visible object is imprinted in the crystalline fluid. We do not hold that view. We say the image is present to the soul without being imprinted or lodged in it, as explained earlier.
Book Four: The Animal Soul and Its Powers
passage-en-00582

Galen's fifth argument is that if an image flowed from the visible object into the crystalline fluid, the object would gradually shrink or disappear. This argument is very weak. Those who support imprinting do not say that anything breaks off from the object and travels to the eye. They say that the crystalline fluid, when facing an object, becomes ready for a matching image to arise in it from its source. That image is what sight perceives.
Book Four: The Animal Soul and Its Powers
passage-en-00583

The sixth argument is that a physical cause cannot act on a distant body without first acting on the nearer body. So if a visible object caused its color and shape to appear in the eye, it should cause them to appear in the air between the object and the eye as well. But our senses show that this does not happen.
Book Four: The Animal Soul and Its Powers
passage-en-00584
The reply is that this would follow only if the nearer body were ready to receive the effect, as the farther one is. The air is not ready to receive an image of the visible object.
Book Four: The Animal Soul and Its Powers
passage-en-00585
VIII. What the ray theorists say
Book Four: The Animal Soul and Its Powers
passage-en-00586

The science of optics and mirrors is a field of its own, studied carefully by many scholars. They base their account on rays leaving the eye and reaching the visible object, just as rays from the sun, moon, and other shining bodies reach what they face. The rays form a cone, with its point at the light source and its base at the object it faces. This suggests that we see by rays leaving the eye, and that we see whatever the rays reach.
Book Four: The Animal Soul and Its Powers
passage-en-00587

But we have proved that what each sense perceives is a perceptual image separate from physical matter, not an image lodged in a physical body. Even so, for sight to occur, the eye must face what gives rise to an image in the perceiving power. The eye is like a point, and when it faces a body, we can imagine a cone between them. We do not deny that rays may extend from the eye toward what is seen. We say only that sight also requires the visible object's image to be present to the soul. Nothing the ray theorists say rules this out. Their account may agree with ours in some of its observations; there is no difficulty in two opposing views sharing some results.
Book Four: The Animal Soul and Its Powers
passage-en-00588

For example, they say that a distant object looks smaller than a nearby one because the cone narrows as it extends outward. The angle at the eye becomes narrower, and the circle at the visible object becomes smaller. The farther away the object is, the smaller these become, until it is too far away to see.
Book Four: The Animal Soul and Its Powers
passage-en-00589

They also say that an object looks larger in water than in air. In air, they say, the rays travel straight. In water, they bend toward the perpendicular and gather together between the water's surface and the object. The object then looks larger because the angle it makes in the crystalline fluid stays wide; the apparent size of the object depends on that angle. Some rays travel straight, while others bend at the water's surface. If the object is close to the surface, the two paths overlap and we see the object across their combined span. If it is farther away, we see it in two separate places, along the straight and bent paths.
Book Four: The Animal Soul and Its Powers
passage-en-00590

They also say that when we open our eyes again after closing them, we may briefly see two moons, as if one were separating from the other. On their account, the rays from the eyes veer away from their usual alignment and cross before reaching the moon. Their ends then fall in two places, so we see two images. They offer the same explanation for people with crossed eyes. They also say that if we place the index and middle fingers against the eye in different positions and look at a lamp, we see two lamps; and that if we look at one of two thin sticks aligned in front of the eye, the other, at a different distance, appears double. They further say that when the moon rises over water, we see one moon in the water by a ray passing into it, and another in the sky by a ray reflected from the water's surface.
Book Four: The Animal Soul and Its Powers
passage-en-00591

Some scholars report their view this way, but there is a problem with it. It is better to say that we see the moon in the sky by a ray reaching it directly, and the image in the water by a ray reflected from the water's surface toward the moon. There is also another effect: in water with a calm, even color, we may see three moons. One is in the sky, seen directly. The other two appear in the water. We see one along a ray reflected from the moon by the water's upper surface; the other is seen along a ray that enters the water, reflects from its curved bottom, and travels back toward the moon.
Book Four: The Animal Soul and Its Powers
passage-en-00592

A similar case occurs when an object appears twice because a mirror is placed between us and it in a certain position: one image is seen directly, and the other along a ray that travels from the eye to the mirror, then reflects toward another object positioned in relation to the mirror as the viewer is.
Book Four: The Animal Soul and Its Powers
passage-en-00593

They also explain why a tree on a riverbank can look upside down in the water. A ray that reaches the water is reflected toward the top of the tree from a point closer to the viewer, and toward the base from a point farther away, until the base of the tree aligns with the base of its reflection. The soul is used to seeing things along straight rays and does not notice the reflection. It therefore takes the reflected ray to have traveled straight through the water. It sees the top as farther away and deeper in the water, and the other parts in order down to the base, so the tree looks inverted. Optics explains these details and similar cases more fully.
Book Four: The Animal Soul and Its Powers
passage-en-00594
IX. Why people see double, and why the ray and imprint views disagree about its cause
Book Four: The Animal Soul and Its Powers
passage-en-00595

Those who support the imprinting view say that the image of a visible object is first imprinted in the crystalline fluid, but sight does not happen there. They say that, just as an imagined cone extends from the visible object and narrows behind the crystalline layer, the image in the crystalline fluid travels through the spirit flowing in the two hollow optic nerves toward their meeting point. The two cones meet and cross there. Beyond that meeting point, there is no perceiving spirit. So the two images join into one at the point where the spirit carries the visual power. If the two images do not reach the same place, but end at different parts of the visual spirit, a separate image comes from each one through the crystalline fluid, and we see one object as two.
Book Four: The Animal Soul and Its Powers
passage-en-00596

The supporters of rays say this explanation fails. If we deliberately cross our eyes and look at something, we also see it double, just as a person with crossed eyes does. But crossing our eyes does not undo the way the two optic nerves meet inside the brain. Their meeting is not something that disappears and reappears at will. They also say that if two objects, one near and one far, are aligned in front of us without the near one blocking the far one, we can focus on the nearer object and see it as one, while the farther one appears double. If we focus on the farther object, the reverse happens. If crossed nerves caused double vision, they say, we could not see one object as single and the other as double at the same time.
Book Four: The Animal Soul and Its Powers
passage-en-00597

They explain it this way. A cone of rays extends from each eye. Within each cone, the ray along its axis is strongest; they call this the ray-line. The two ray-lines meet at the object we focus on. When we focus on the nearer object, the two lines meet there. The farther object then lies away from each line, toward the outer edge of both cones. We see the nearer object as one because the two lines meet on it, while the farther one appears twice: the ray from the right eye falls to its left, and the ray from the left eye falls to its right. When we focus on the farther object, the two lines meet there, and they fall on two different places on the nearer object, so the farther one appears single and the nearer one double.
Book Four: The Animal Soul and Its Powers
passage-en-00598

The same applies to someone with crossed eyes. The main rays from the two eyes do not meet at one point; each falls on the nearby side of the cone's base, or they cross in the air before reaching the object. Such people usually see things with the edge of the cone rather than with its central ray. If they can make the two central rays meet on one object, they see it as one, as it is.
Book Four: The Animal Soul and Its Powers
passage-en-00599

Those who support imprinting have offered other explanations for double vision. One is that the visual spirit moves to the right or left, so the image is formed in one place before the two cones cross, and the object appears twice. This is like seeing one reflection in still water and many reflections in rippling water. Another explanation is that the spirit behind the crossing of the optic nerves moves forward or backward. In that case, it has two opposite movements: one toward the shared sense and the other toward the meeting point of the nerves. The image reaches both before the earlier image has faded, so each place receives another visible image. The difference between the explanations is that the first describes movement from side to side, while the second describes movement forward and back.
Book Four: The Animal Soul and Its Powers
passage-en-00600
X. Why sight needs a transparent medium
Book Four: The Animal Soul and Its Powers
passage-en-00601

Here is the argument. A power that belongs to a body can affect something, or be affected by it, only through a shared position. Action and reaction take place between things linked as cause and effect. This link is direct between a power and the matter, subject, or body it belongs to, since these help make it what it is, set it apart, or complete it. The link is indirect between that power and something else that has a spatial relation to its body.
Book Four: The Animal Soul and Its Powers
passage-en-00602

For bodies, their position relative to one another matters, much as the relation between cause and effect matters for things that do not depend on matter. Position is a way a body exists and is set apart from other bodies. If two bodies touch and join at their edges, they can act as if they were one body.
Book Four: The Animal Soul and Its Powers
passage-en-00603

So if something outside one of them affects it, the effect can pass to the other. When fire heats one part of a body, another connected part also warms. When light shines on one surface, it can light a second surface placed in line with the first. I have specified an outside effect because an inward action that does not depend on position does not pass to a neighboring thing.
Book Four: The Animal Soul and Its Powers
passage-en-00604

With this in mind, we can say that sensing—including sight—is the sense power's being affected by an external physical thing. So there must be a spatial link between the bodily basis of the sense power and the thing it senses. Facing each other is not enough if no physical body lies between them: without some contact or connection in space, there is no natural link. The link must be either a mental relation or a physical connection. So a body must join the sense organ and the object.
Book Four: The Animal Soul and Its Powers
passage-en-00605

If that body were dense, thick, and dark, it could not receive light. How then could it connect the visible object to the eye, or the light source to the thing lit? A link between two things must help their action, not block it. So the body between them must be transparent and must not block light, whether light travels from its source to the lit thing, from the eye to what is seen, or as an image from the object to the eye.
Book Four: The Animal Soul and Its Powers
passage-en-00606

This shows why the claim that a thinner medium is always better cannot be right. If an empty space lay between the eye and the object, sight would be even stronger, and we might see an ant in the sky. It is not enough to answer that this is impossible, and that making the medium thinner does not always make sight stronger. If the medium needs to be thin so light can pass through, then removing it altogether should make light pass even more easily. The flaw is that thinness does not mean the medium can be absent. If no physical body joined the viewer and the object, there would be no action between them.
Book Four: The Animal Soul and Its Powers
passage-en-00607

You might say that the Shaykh admits this kind of action does not require the cause and the thing affected to touch. If there were empty space between the sense and the object, what would be wrong with an image being imprinted in the sense? The answer is that even without direct touch, there must still be either contact or a physical medium between them. That medium and the thing affected must work together almost as one body: one part is ready to receive the effect, while the other is not. If there were no body between fire and what it heats, nothing would warm. And if there were no body between the sun and the earth, the earth would receive neither light nor heat.
Book Four: The Animal Soul and Its Powers
passage-en-00608
XI. Why there are only five senses
Book Four: The Animal Soul and Its Powers
passage-en-00609

Most people thought there might be a sixth sense in addition to the five. The philosophers denied it. They argued, as the Shaykh explains in one of his books, that nature does not move from a simpler kind to a more complete kind until it has brought the simpler kind to its full development. In the same way, nature could not rise above animal life without first completing all the powers of animals. If another sense were possible, animals would have it. Since even the human being, the most complete animal we know, does not have a sixth sense, there is no other sense.
Book Four: The Animal Soul and Its Powers
passage-en-00610
XII. What the senses have in common
Book Four: The Animal Soul and Its Powers
passage-en-00611

Some people say that the only things we directly sense are qualities sensed through the body, such as colors, sounds, smells, tastes, and things felt by touch. Everything else is sensed only indirectly. On this view, the senses have no thing they can sense in common. That is not so.
Book Four: The Animal Soul and Its Powers
passage-en-00612

By something sensed directly, I mean something that leaves an effect in the sense power. Something sensed indirectly does not do this. It is not truly sensed; it is simply linked to what we do sense. For example, when we see Abu Zayd, the person himself is what we really see, because his image reaches our sight. But we do not see that he is a father. No image of fatherhood enters the sense. The mind works out that relation by comparing him with his child.
Book Four: The Animal Soul and Its Powers
passage-en-00613

Magnitude, number, position, motion and rest, nearness and distance, touching and being apart are different. We may not sense them on their own, but we do sense them together with something else: with color and light in sight, with heat and moisture in touch, and with other qualities through the other senses. A thing does not stop being directly sensed just because we need to sense something else at the same time. What matters is whether the thing itself makes an impression on the sense, not whether another feature helps us notice it.
Book Four: The Animal Soul and Its Powers
passage-en-00614

So anything we call sensed either does or does not leave an effect in the sense. If it does not, it is sensed only indirectly. If it does, then sensing it either depends on sensing something else or does not. If it depends on another sensed thing, it is something sensed through another quality; if it does not, it is sensed on its own. I say this is true when we look at the question broadly. On closer examination, what is directly sensed is the image present to the soul, not the external thing that matches it.
Book Four: The Animal Soul and Its Powers
passage-en-00615

Sight senses size, number, shape, position, motion, and rest through color. Some people say motion and rest are not sensed. They argue that someone sitting on a fast-moving ship does not feel the ship move. They also say rest is an absence, so how could it be sensed?
Book Four: The Animal Soul and Its Powers
passage-en-00616

Understand that motion and rest are sensed when the mind recognizes them with help from the senses. The sense sees a body first near one thing, then farther from it, and continues to register that change. The mind then judges that the body has moved. The idea of something moving from possibility to reality is not itself sensed; it describes a relation. In the same way, the sense sees a body staying in one place, and the mind judges that it is at rest. The sense does not itself perceive that the body has stayed still or failed to move, because one idea is a relation and the other is an absence. Neither is sensed on its own. A person on a ship does not feel it move when the senses register no change in its position compared with something outside it. So motion and rest seem to be judgments of the mind made with help from the senses, as sight is.
Book Four: The Animal Soul and Its Powers
passage-en-00617

Touch also senses all the things listed above through hardness and softness, heat and cold, and other qualities. Taste senses flavor; through flavor it can sense amount by tasting more or less, and number by tasting different flavors. It senses motion and rest only weakly, and then only with help from touch. Smell senses none of these except number, with help from the mind: we know that a smell that has stopped is not the same as one that later returns. Hearing does not sense size, but it helps the mind judge that loud sounds usually come from large bodies. In general, sight senses these shared features more clearly, though the mind helps here too.
Book Four: The Animal Soul and Its Powers
passage-en-00618

If you want the deeper truth, no act of sensing stands on its own without imagination, and no act of imagination stands on its own without thought. Sense could not exist apart from thought, and it cannot be separated from thought in the way a hammer or chisel can exist without a carpenter. Human hearing and sight cannot be understood apart from the thinking power; in other animals, they cannot be understood apart from the animal soul. The soul cannot exist apart from intellect, and intellect cannot exist apart from God. This has carried us beyond the subject at hand, though we have touched on it before.
Book Four: The Animal Soul and Its Powers
passage-en-00619

If this is how the senses work, then the same is true of the things they sense. Everything sensed is also understood by the intellect, in the basic sense that the intellect ultimately knows it. By convention, however, we call the particular knowledge gained through the senses “sensing,” to distinguish it from the intellect's knowledge of general ideas.
Book Four: The Animal Soul and Its Powers
passage-en-00620

Some people think animals need another sense, beyond the five, to perceive these shared features. That is mistaken. As we have seen, each of the five senses can perceive them. There is no need for a sixth. A sixth sense would add nothing, since the five already do this work, and nature does not create a power that serves no purpose.
Book Five: The soul’s inner perceptions
passage-en-00621
Book Five: The soul’s inner perceptions
Book Five: The soul’s inner perceptions
passage-en-00622
I. Common sense, or the soul’s tablet
Book Five: The soul’s inner perceptions
passage-en-00623

Most people say that common sense is a power located in the front part of the brain. I hold that it is a power of the soul, prepared to arise in the front of the brain, more precisely in the vital spirit that flows there. It receives the forms carried to it by all the outer senses. The senses are like spies who bring reports from distant regions to the king’s minister.
Book Five: The soul’s inner perceptions
passage-en-00624

They offer three arguments for this power. The first is that we judge, for example, that this white thing is sweet, or that this is not that thing. Anyone who judges between two things must have both before them. The judge cannot be the intellect alone, without the help of a sense. First, we perceive sensible things only through particular organs. Second, animals without reason make such judgments too; without them, they could not stay alive. If smell and shape did not tell an animal what it should seek, or what it should flee, it would neither pursue nor avoid anything. So the things perceived by the outer senses must come together in one particular power of perception. Since none of the outer senses does this, there must be an inner power that perceives particulars. This is what we call common sense.
Book Five: The soul’s inner perceptions
passage-en-00625

This argument is not decisive. In human beings, the intellect gathers and directs all the powers of perception; in animals, estimation does this. Either can judge what the senses perceive. To judge that sugar is white and sweet, for example, it is enough to see its whiteness and taste its sweetness.
Book Five: The soul’s inner perceptions
passage-en-00626

There is another case. We first understand the general idea of a human being, then see a particular person and judge, “This person is human.” The general idea is understood by the intellect; the individual person is perceived by the senses. If a judge must directly perceive both things being compared, then we would need a third power, one that perceives both general ideas and particular things. The intellect perceives general ideas, while the senses perceive particular things. So either this judgment would be impossible, or there would have to be another power that is neither intellect nor sense. Both conclusions are false, so the argument does not hold.
Book Five: The soul’s inner perceptions
passage-en-00627

Bahmanyār says that the power that judges that a certain taste belongs to something of a certain color need not itself perceive the sensible forms, just as the power of desire need not perceive the things that stir it. The soul can taste the flavor and see the color, while another power judges that this flavor belongs to something of this color. I find no fault with this. A critic objects that every judgment requires us to understand both things being judged: how could someone judge that the world is created without first understanding both “world” and “created”? But by “another power,” Bahmanyār means a power that perceives, such as the intellect in a human being and estimation in other animals. His point is that once taste has made the flavor known and sight has made the color known, the intellect or estimation can judge that this flavor belongs to the thing of that color. So there is no judgment without the two things being understood.
Book Five: The soul’s inner perceptions
passage-en-00628

When philosophers say that the intellect does not perceive particular things, they mean that it does not perceive them on its own, without a perceptual power such as the senses. And when they say estimation does not perceive what the outer senses perceive, they mean it cannot do so on its own, without those senses. In human beings, the intellect is ultimately the power that knows both general ideas and particulars. In other animals, estimation is the power that knows both what they sense and what they infer from it. This objection comes from not following the philosophers’ terms closely enough.
Book Five: The soul’s inner perceptions
passage-en-00629

The second argument is that a falling raindrop looks like a straight line, and a spark moving around on a spinning wheel looks like a circle, even though the drop itself is not a line and the spark itself is not a circle. These images must therefore appear in a particular power other than sight. This seems clear whether we think that sight sends out rays toward an object or that the object’s image reaches the eye. In the latter view, the material object must be present for us to see it. But the line and circle we see are not the forms of the object where it is now. So these images must appear in another particular power, not in the eye.
Book Five: The soul’s inner perceptions
passage-en-00630

The author of Eastern Discussions objects that this argument first assumes that an image is imprinted in the eye, then uses that assumption to prove that an image is imprinted in common sense. Why could the image not remain in the visual spirit for a while? As the raindrop moves from one place to another, its image might be imprinted at each place in turn. Before the first image disappears, a second is made. When the two images are present together, sight perceives a point as a line. Avicenna also accepts that sight perceives motion, and motion could not be perceived unless this happened.
Book Five: The soul’s inner perceptions
passage-en-00631

I reply that I have already shown, without relying on this argument, that seeing requires an image of the thing to be present to the soul. But it is not possible for the eye to retain these imprints and perceive a point as a line. Sight is a bodily power; it perceives only things that share a position with it. A thing that has no position in relation to the sense organ cannot affect it or leave an impression on it. The raindrop is in one place at a time. Once it has moved, it is no longer in its earlier place; what is no longer there has no position and cannot affect a bodily power.
Book Five: The soul’s inner perceptions
passage-en-00632

If sight could perceive the image of a point in a position after the point had left that position, it would perceive something absent without a cause. It would also mean that the outer senses could perceive things that are no longer present. But perceiving absent things belongs to the inner senses, since those things are not imprinted in matter. We know by experience that the outer senses do not perceive the past or the future: sight cannot see a color that was present yesterday, and smell cannot detect a scent that will be present tomorrow. The same is true here.
Book Five: The soul’s inner perceptions
passage-en-00633

As for Avicenna’s claim that sight perceives motion, I have already explained that the intellect recognizes motion by comparing what the senses register. Sight does not perceive every part of a movement in a single, instant act. If all the stages of a movement were imprinted at once, as with a falling drop or a moving spark, that would happen in common sense, not in the outer sense of sight.
Book Five: The soul’s inner perceptions
passage-en-00634

The third argument, and in my view the strongest, is that we perceive images that do not exist outside us. People suffering from delirium may see them, as may people in dreams. They see large, distinct figures and hear sounds unlike ordinary ones. Prophets and saints, peace be upon them, may also see beautiful forms and hear sounds that they recognize as different from ordinary sensory experiences, even when their senses are clear. People whose minds are overwhelmed by fear or shock—in war, earthquakes, and other crises—may see images that reflect what they are going through, as their souls turn away from the outer world.
Book Five: The soul’s inner perceptions
passage-en-00635

These images must exist in some way, since pure nothingness cannot be distinguished from anything else. Yet they do not exist outside us; if they did, anyone with sound senses would see them. Nor does the intellect perceive them, since it does not grasp bodies, dimensions, and shapes as particulars. The outer senses cannot be their source either: such images usually appear when the senses are quiet or inactive, as in sleep, and some are seen while awake with the eyes closed.
Book Five: The soul’s inner perceptions
passage-en-00636

The power that perceives them must therefore be an inner one, distinct from the intellect. It cannot be imagination, since imagination preserves images rather than perceiving them. If it perceived every image it preserved, then everything stored in it would always be present to view, which is not the case. So there must be another power: common sense. It is connected with the front part of the brain, in the first ventricle, and its perceptions appear through the vital spirit there. This spirit is like a mirror. It has no colors of its own, yet it can show the colors of things without having their images imprinted in it. In the same way, because it is clear and balanced, the vital spirit allows unseen images resembling things we sense to appear to the soul. The soul perceives them through this power, which lets it perceive what the outer senses cannot reach. This is what we set out to show.
Book Five: The soul’s inner perceptions
passage-en-00637

Those who deny the existence of this power offer two arguments. First, someone asleep may see a mountain made of ruby or a sea of fire. Such enormous images could not be imprinted in the small mass of the brain; the large cannot be imprinted in the small. Their home must therefore be the soul itself, not another power, so the claim that common sense exists is false. Second, we know by experience that we do not taste or touch with our hands or feet. We know just as certainly that we do not taste or touch with the brain.
Book Five: The soul’s inner perceptions
passage-en-00638

I reply that the first objection does not apply to my view. I do not say that perceived images are physically imprinted in a body. They belong to the soul in another way, not by being physically lodged in it. The second objection also misses the point. The brain is not where the images are imprinted. Nor does the soul need the brain in order to perceive images it has received through the senses, or to perceive absent things once it is prepared to do so. The brain is needed as the place where this power can arise and as the bodily basis that prepares the soul to connect with the source from which images take shape. I firmly deny that these enormous images are imprinted in any part of the brain. We have shown that images of imagination do not exist in this physical world, since they do not have positions in space. Still, another power besides the soul itself must be established, because the one that perceives particulars is different from the one that perceives universals. A particular thing and a universal idea are different in kind, and the perceiver must be of the same kind as what it perceives. So the power that perceives particulars cannot be the one that perceives universals.

II. Imagination
Book Five: The soul’s inner perceptions
passage-en-00640
Imagination, also called the formative power, is the power that preserves images within us. Three arguments are offered to show that it differs from common sense.
Book Five: The soul’s inner perceptions
passage-en-00641

First, common sense can receive images, while imagination preserves them. Receiving and preserving are different powers. Water can take the shape of a vessel without keeping that shape once the vessel is removed. If receiving and preserving were one and the same power, they could not come apart as they do here. The second difference is that receiving is a capacity to take on an image, while preserving is an established ability to hold it. These are opposite aspects of the same subject. The objection that this reasoning relies on the rule “one thing cannot produce more than one thing” comes from a lack of care and understanding, as we have already explained.
Book Five: The soul’s inner perceptions
passage-en-00642

The second argument is that common sense judges the things it perceives and assents to them, while imagination does not judge; it only preserves. A single power cannot both judge and refrain from judging. The objection is: why could the same power not judge at one time and preserve at another?
Book Five: The soul’s inner perceptions
passage-en-00643

The third argument is that images of things we sense can be present to us directly, or they can be imagined. Seeing an image and imagining it are different, so the powers that do them must differ. The author of Eastern Discussions objects that we may not always be attending to the intelligible images we know. Where are they stored while we are not thinking of them? If the answer is that they come from the source that gives them when the soul turns toward it, and disappear when the soul turns away, then why could imagined images not work the same way? When common sense is ready to bring them to mind, why could they not flow to it from the source of images?
Book Five: The soul’s inner perceptions
passage-en-00644

I answer that a power with an established ability to turn toward, or connect with, a source that gives images can receive them without having to acquire them anew through thought or sensation. This is different from a power without that established ability, which must work to perceive an image—through sensation, as with common sense, or through thought, as with the soul. The soul cannot call up what it has not yet learned whenever it chooses. It needs to search and acquire knowledge, unless it has gained an intellectual habit through repeated acts of perception, thought, and reflection. The strength of that habit is a lasting intellectual light received from its source, which in my view is a being above the soul and below the active intellect.
Book Five: The soul’s inner perceptions
passage-en-00645

The same applies here. At first, perceiving a sensible image requires something that brings it to us, such as a sense. Preserving it requires a further, established ability in the power that perceives it. That ability lets us call back images we have forgotten, even after their causes have disappeared from the senses.
Book Five: The soul’s inner perceptions
passage-en-00646

We have already shown that the power that calls back images is not found in material things. Still, it is not essential to our philosophical account to prove that common sense and imagination are different powers. Even if they were one power with a less developed and a more developed side, nothing important would be lost. What matters is to establish that this is an inner, substantial power, distinct from intellect and the outer senses, with a realm of its own beyond the world of intellect and the world of nature and motion. We have already proved that it is not part of the body or its parts. Through it, the states of the grave, its reward and punishment, the intermediate realm, and the resurrection of bodies become real. Its domain is the whole body, its authority is in the rear of the first brain ventricle, and its instrument is the vital spirit located there.
Book Five: The soul’s inner perceptions
passage-en-00647
III. Imagination, estimation, and memory
Book Five: The soul’s inner perceptions
passage-en-00648

The imaginative power is also called the thinking power when the rational soul uses it to arrange thoughts and their premises. It differs from the other powers of perception because acting and arranging are different from perceiving and judging. We can combine images we have sensed or separate them in a way we have never seen outside us—for example, we can imagine an animal with a human head, a horse’s body, and two wings. None of the other powers does this, so it must belong to a different power.
Book Five: The soul’s inner perceptions
passage-en-00649

An objection follows: if this power perceives, then one and the same thing both perceives and rearranges images. If it does not perceive, then how can it rearrange the images and separate or combine them? This would contradict the claim that anyone judging two things must have both present to the mind.
Book Five: The soul’s inner perceptions
passage-en-00650

In addition, estimation uses the imaginative power, which would mean that estimation both perceives and rearranges images. Tusi answers the first objection by saying that this power does not perceive; it only has the two things present as it works with them. Not everything present to a power must be something it perceives. He answers the second objection by saying that one thing can perceive and act in different ways—through itself and through an instrument, or through two different instruments. The imaginative power is located in the front part of the brain’s middle ventricle. It serves estimation and, through estimation, the intellect.
Book Five: The soul’s inner perceptions
passage-en-00651

The estimative power is said to differ from the other powers because we judge what we perceive by meanings that we do not sense directly and that have no physical image. Some meanings are not the kind that can be sensed at all, such as the hostility a sheep perceives in a wolf or the affection a young lamb perceives in its mother. Other meanings can be sensed, but we may judge them without sensing them at that moment. For example, seeing something yellow may lead us to judge that it is honey and sweet, even though we have not tasted it. The power that perceives these meanings is called estimation. It perceives the first kind—the meanings tied to particular things—on its own. It perceives the second kind, images not currently present, by using the formative power. None of the powers we have mentioned can do this, since they perceive only sensible images, whereas estimation perceives meanings. It is therefore another power. The whole brain is involved in its work, but it is especially connected with the middle ventricle.
Book Five: The soul’s inner perceptions
passage-en-00652

In my view, although estimation differs from the powers just mentioned, it is not a separate being from the intellect. It is the intellect turned toward a particular person or thing, concerned with it and directing it. The intellect connected with imagination is what we call estimation. What it perceives are general meanings attached to images of particular things. Estimation has no existence of its own apart from the intellect, just as a general nature, such as humanity, has no existence apart from actual human beings or the intellect’s understanding of it.
Book Five: The soul’s inner perceptions
passage-en-00653

Here is the argument. When estimation perceives the hostility of a particular animal, either it perceives hostility apart from that animal or it perceives hostility only as belonging to that individual. If it is the first, then it has perceived the general idea of hostility, and estimation is simply intellect. If it is the second, then it is clear to the intellect that hostility is not a physical quality residing in that animal. If it were, it would be sensed like the animal’s existence or unity. Perceiving its hostility would then be an act of sense, not estimation.
Book Five: The soul’s inner perceptions
passage-en-00654

In general, when an intelligible meaning is found in particular things, it is there in one of two ways. It may be a meaning the mind draws from those things, such as cause and effect, before and after, and other relations such as parent and child. Or it may have a sensible form in those things, such as blackness, smell, or taste.
Book Five: The soul’s inner perceptions
passage-en-00655

The first kind is perceived by intellect alone when considered apart from what it relates to, and by estimation when it is tied to one or more particular things. The second kind is perceived by one of the senses or by imagination. Hostility is of the first kind. Even when tied to a particular, it remains a general meaning joined to that particular; it does not physically reside in a body. Estimation perceives a general meaning qualified by something particular. As mentioned above, the other class is perceived by intellect or by one of the senses.
Book Five: The soul’s inner perceptions
passage-en-00656

The power of memory is said to be a storehouse for estimation, just as imagination is a storehouse for common sense. It holds images of the meanings estimation perceives. It is also called the power of recollection because it can bring those meanings back.
Book Five: The soul’s inner perceptions
passage-en-00657

Recollection sometimes moves from an image to its meaning. Estimation, helped by the imaginative power, looks through the images held in imagination until it finds the image that was present when it first perceived a given meaning. Then the meaning stored in memory comes back to mind.
Book Five: The soul’s inner perceptions
passage-en-00658

At other times, recollection moves from a meaning to its image. The power looks through the meanings stored in memory until it finds the one that was perceived together with the image being sought. If that does not work—because the image has faded from imagination or some other obstacle gets in the way—we need to sense it again.
Book Five: The soul’s inner perceptions
passage-en-00659
The outer sense then supplies the image, imagination stores it, and the meaning held in memory returns.
Book Five: The soul’s inner perceptions
passage-en-00660

Some object that preserving meanings differs from perceiving them, and perceiving them differs from searching through them. So recollection must involve separate powers for preserving, perceiving, and searching. That would bring the number of inner powers above the five already mentioned. The answer is that estimation perceives, memory preserves, and the thinking power searches and arranges. These three powers are enough for recollection; no further power is needed. Recollection is one name for their combined work, not a single power in its own right. Remembering likewise combines perception with preservation.
Book Five: The soul’s inner perceptions
passage-en-00661

These powers differ in their existence and may develop at different times. Some animals have only outer sensation; others have imagination but no estimation; others lack memory. Yet when fully developed, they return to one underlying self with many ways of acting. I will explain later how the soul itself perceives both particular images and general meanings. I have already offered many hints that can lead a thoughtful reader to this point, but I will make the matter clearer, since it is a profound subject and a precious one.
Book Five: The soul’s inner perceptions
passage-en-00662

Avicenna also says in The Canon that there is a philosophical question here: are preservation, recollection, and the recovery of meanings lost from memory one power or two? He adds that a physician does not need to settle it. He does not decide between difference and unity because either way, the answer is not needed for medicine. A physician is not required to know this. For them, the powers of estimation and memory act in one brain region, or in regions so closely joined that an injury to one affects the other.
Book Five: The soul’s inner perceptions
passage-en-00663

A theoretical question needs proof, and medical evidence cannot settle it. A full explanation would belong to another field, beyond medicine. Yet in The Healing, Avicenna says that the same power is also called remembering: it preserves what it has, recalls it when ready, and brings it back when it has been lost. Estimation then uses its imaginative power to present images one by one until the needed one appears. This suggests that the two are one power. But, as we have seen, remembering involves two acts, while recollection involves three. Their unity is therefore a unity in name and function, as is the unity of the power from which they arise. There is more to say about this, and I will return to it.
Book Five: The soul’s inner perceptions
passage-en-00664

Avicenna supports this view in The Healing. Near the end of his discussion of the soul’s powers, he says that the estimative power may be the very same power as the thinking, imaginative, and remembering powers, and as the power that judges. It judges by its own nature, and imagines and remembers through its movements and actions. It imagines through what it does with images and meanings, and remembers through the result of that work. Memory is the storehouse in which these are kept.
Book Five: The soul’s inner perceptions
passage-en-00665

This does not conflict with what Avicenna says just before this passage; it supports it. He says that the power that combines image with image, image with meaning, or meaning with meaning seems to be the estimative power in its location—not in its role as judge, but in its work of reaching a judgment. He places it in the middle of the brain so that it can reach both storehouses, for images and for meanings. This shows that the source of thinking, remembering, imagining, and preserving is one in its underlying identity, though it branches into different powers according to its changing states and levels.
Book Five: The soul’s inner perceptions
passage-en-00666

There is no real inconsistency in Avicenna’s words, as some have thought. In his view, these powers are distinct but depend on one another, and all are instruments of estimation. Their actions belong to them as a tool’s action belongs to the tool: strictly speaking, the action belongs to the one using the tool, not to the tool itself. Estimation, in turn, is an instrument of intellect in beings that have intellect.
Book Five: The soul’s inner perceptions
passage-en-00667

But Avicenna and his followers did not hold that all powers of perception and movement, despite their differences, are one individual reality whose unity gathers all their meanings and identities. Listen closely to what is revealed from the world of mysteries, and guard it from those who are not ready to hear it.

IV. The soul as the source of all our powers
Book Five: The soul’s inner perceptions
passage-en-00669

By this I mean that the one who perceives through all the powers of a human being is the rational soul. It is also what moves the body through the powers found in animals, plants, and nature. This is a profound point, and there are many arguments for it. Some begin from perception, others from movement. I will give three arguments from perception first.
Book Five: The soul’s inner perceptions
passage-en-00670

The first begins with what we know. We can compare what we see, feel, imagine, and understand. For example, we can say that something with this color has this taste, or that something with this sound has this smell. To make a judgment between two things, both must be present to the one who judges. To accept or reject a claim, we must first understand both sides. So there must be one power that can perceive all the things the outer senses perceive. Otherwise, we could not judge that this color belongs to this taste, or that this sound belongs to this smell.
Book Five: The soul’s inner perceptions
passage-en-00671

The same is true when we imagine a face and then see it with our eyes. We can judge that the imagined face is the face of the person we see, Zayd, for example. One power must perceive both the imagined form and the image we see, so it can judge whether one matches the other. The same happens when we recognize Zayd’s hostility or ‘Amr’s affection: an image we see and a meaning we infer come together in us.
Book Five: The soul’s inner perceptions
passage-en-00672

We can also combine or separate imagined forms and particular meanings, bring them together or distinguish them, and judge that one belongs to another—or does not. Any judgment requires both what is being judged and what is said of it to be present. So the power that combines or separates meanings and forms must perceive both.
